source_text: Ὥστε τὸ ἐπὶ πλέον κατέχειν, ἐπὶ πλέον ἐστὶν ὑμᾶς τῶν κακῶν ὑπεξάγειν. Ἱκανὰ [καὶ] τὰ εἰρημένα εὐγνώμονι κριτῇ, ἐὰν μή τις πρὸς τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς κτίσεως ἀποβλέπῃ, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ τῆς ἡμετέρας δυνάμεως ἀσθενὲς, καὶ πρὸς τὸ αὔταρκες εἰς εὐφροσύνην τῶν συνεληλυθότων. Ἡ γῆ ὑμᾶς ταῖς οἰκείαις βλάσταις ἐδεξιώσατο· ἡ θάλασσα τοῖς ἰχθύσιν, ὁ ἀὴρ τοῖς πτηνοῖς. Ἑτοίμη ἡ χέρσος, ὁμότιμα τούτοις ἀντε πιδείξασθαι. Ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μέτρον ἔστω τῆς ἑωθινῆς ἑστιά σεως, ἵνα μὴ ὁ ὑπερβάλλων κόρος ἀμβλυτέρους ὑμᾶς πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἑσπερινῶν ἀπόλαυσιν καταστήσῃ. Ὁ δὲ τὰ πάντα πληρώσας τῆς ἑαυτοῦ κτίσεως, καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ἡμῖν τῶν οἰκείων θαυμάτων ἐναργῆ τὰ ὑπομνήματα καταλιπὼν, πληρώσαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας πάσης εὐφροσύνης πνευματικῆς, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος, εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν. ΟΜΙΛΙΑ θʹ Περὶ χερσαίων. 9.1 Πῶς ὑμῖν ἡ ἑωθινὴ τῶν λόγων τράπεζα κατεφάνη; Ἐμοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἐπῆλθεν εἰκάσαι τὰ ἐμαυτοῦ πένητός τινος ἑστιάτορος φιλοφροσύνῃ, ὃς τῶν εὐτραπέζων τις εἶναι φιλοτιμούμενος, ἀπορίᾳ τῶν πολυτελεστέρων ἀποκναίει τοὺς δαιτυμόνας, τὴν πενιχρὰν παρασκευὴν δαψιλῶς ἐπιφέρων τῇ τραπέζῃ· ὥστε περιίστασθαι αὐτῷ εἰς ἀπειροκαλίας ὄνειδος τὸ φιλότιμον. Τοιοῦτον δή τι καὶ τὸ ἡμέτερον, εἰ μή τι ὑμεῖς ἄλλο λέγετε. Πλὴν ὁποῖά ποτ' ἂν ᾖ, οὐκ ἐξουδενωτέον ὑμῖν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ Ἐλισσαῖον ὡς φαῦλον ἑστιάτορα παρῃτοῦντο οἱ τότε, καὶ ταῦτα λαχάνοις ἀγρίοις ἑστιῶντα τοὺς φίλους. Οἶδα νόμους ἀλληγορίας, εἰ καὶ μὴ παρ' ἐμαυτοῦ ἐξευρὼν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς παρ' ἑτέρων πεπονημένοις περιτυχών. Ἃς οἱ μὴ καταδεχόμενοι τὰς κοινὰς τῶν γεγραμ μένων ἐννοίας, τὸ ὕδωρ οὐχ ὕδωρ λέγουσιν, ἀλλά τινα ἄλλην φύσιν, καὶ φυτὸν καὶ ἰχθὺν πρὸς τὸ ἑαυτοῖς δοκοῦν ἑρμηνεύουσι, καὶ ἑρπετῶν γένεσιν καὶ θηρίων ἐπὶ τὰς οἰκείας ὑπονοίας παρατρέψαντες ἐξηγοῦνται, ὥσπερ οἱ ὀνειροκρίται τῶν φανέντων ἐν ταῖς καθ' ὕπνον φαντασίαις πρὸς τὸν οἰκεῖον σκοπὸν τὰς ἐξηγήσεις ποιούμενοι. Ἐγὼ δὲ χόρτον ἀκούσας, χόρτον νοῶ, καὶ φυτὸν, καὶ ἰχθὺν, καὶ θηρίον, καὶ κτῆνος, πάντα ὡς εἴρηται οὕτως ἐκδέχομαι. Καὶ γὰρ οὐκ ἐπαισχύνομαι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον. Οὐδὲ ἐπειδὴ οἱ τὰ περὶ κόσμου γράψαντες πολλὰ περὶ σχημάτων γῆς διελέχθησαν, εἴτε σφαῖρά ἐστιν, εἴτε κύλινδρος, εἴτε καὶ δίσκῳ ἐστὶν ἐμφερὴς ἡ γῆ, καὶ ἐξίσου πάντοθεν ἀποτετόρνευται, ἢ λικνοειδής ἐστι, καὶ μεσόκοιλος (πρὸς πάσας γὰρ ταύτας τὰς ὑπονοίας οἱ τὰ περὶ τοῦ κόσμου γράψαντες ὑπηνέχθησαν, τὰ ἀλλήλων ἕκαστος καταλύοντες), οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο προαχθήσομαι ἀτιμοτέραν εἰπεῖν τὴν ἡμετέραν κοσμοποιίαν, ἐπειδὴ οὐδὲν περὶ σχημάτων ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ θεράπων Μωϋσῆς διελέχθη, οὐδὲ εἶπε δέκα καὶ ὀκτὼ μυριάδας σταδίων τὸ περίμετρον ἔχειν τῆς γῆς· καὶ τὸ ἀπ' αὐτῆς σκίασμα, ἐν τῇ ὑπὸ γῆν τοῦ ἡλίου κινήσει, ἐπὶ πόσον χωρεῖ τοῦ ἀέρος οὐ διεμέτρησε· καὶ πῶς τοῦτο τῇ σελήνῃ προσενεχθὲν τὰς ἐκλείψεις ποιεῖ. Ἐπειδὴ τὰ μηδὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς ὡς ἄχρηστα ἡμῖν ἀπεσιώπησεν· ἆρα τούτου ἕνεκεν ἀτιμότερα ἡγήσομαι τῆς μωρανθείσης σοφίας τὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος λόγια; ἢ μᾶλλον δοξάσω τὸν μὴ ἀπασχολήσαντα τὸν νοῦν ἡμῶν ἐπὶ τὰ μάταια, ἀλλὰ πάντα εἰς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ καταρτισμὸν τῶν ψυχῶν ἡμῶν γραφῆναι οἰκονομήσαντα; Ὅ μοι δοκοῦσι μὴ συνειδότες τινὲς, παραγωγαῖς τισι καὶ τροπολογίαις σεμνότητά τινα ἐκ τῆς οἰκείας αὐτῶν διανοίας ἐπεχείρησαν τοῖς γεγραμμένοις ἐπιφημίσαι.
thought_title: Defense of literal reading of creation
orientation: Basil is closing the eighth homily and opening the ninth, defending his literal reading of Genesis against allegorizers.
pass_a_gloss: So that to hold you longer is to draw you away from evils more. The things said are sufficient for a fair judge, unless someone looks not at the wealth of creation, but at the weakness of our power, and at what is sufficient for the joy of those assembled. The earth welcomed you with its own shoots; the sea with fish, the air with birds. The dry land is ready to display things of equal honor to these. But let this be the measure of the morning feast, so that excessive satiety may not make you duller for the enjoyment of the evening things. May he who filled all things with his own creation, and left in all things clear memorials of his own wonders for us, fill your hearts with all spiritual joy, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be the glory and the power, to the ages of ages. Amen. Homily 9, On land animals. 9.1 How did the morning table of words appear to you? For it occurred to me to liken my own things to the friendliness of some poor host, who, being eager to be one of the well-furnished hosts, by lack of more costly things wears out the guests, bringing the poor preparation abundantly to the table; so that his eagerness turns around into a reproach of tastelessness for him. Such indeed is also our case, unless you say something else. But whatever sort it may be, it must not be despised by you. For neither did those of that time reject Elisha as a poor host, and that when he was feasting his friends with wild vegetables. I know the laws of allegory, even if not having discovered them from myself, but having encountered the things labored over by others. Those who do not accept the common meanings of the things written say that water is not water, but some other nature, and they interpret plant and fish according to what seems good to themselves, and they explain the origin of reptiles and wild beasts by twisting them to their own suppositions, just as dream interpreters make their explanations of the things appearing in sleep visions according to their own aim. But I, when I hear grass, understand grass, and plant, and fish, and wild beast, and cattle, all things as they are said, so I receive them. For I am not ashamed of the gospel. Nor because those who wrote about the world discussed many things about the shapes of the earth, whether the earth is a sphere, or a cylinder, or is also like a disk, and is turned equally from all sides, or is winnowing-fan-shaped, and hollow in the middle (for to all these suppositions those who wrote about the world were carried, each destroying the things of the others), will I for this reason be led to call our world-making more dishonorable, because the servant of God Moses discussed nothing about shapes, nor did he say that the circumference of the earth has one hundred and eighty thousand stades; and he did not measure how far its shadow, in the movement of the sun under the earth, goes through the air; and how this, brought to the moon, makes the eclipses. Since he passed over in silence the things that are nothing to us as useless to us; shall I for this reason consider the oracles of the Spirit more dishonorable than the wisdom that has been made foolish? Or rather shall I glorify the one who did not occupy our mind with vain things, but arranged all things to be written for building up and equipping of our souls? Which some, it seems to me, not having understood, attempted by certain distortions and figurative turns to attach some solemnity from their own thought to the things written.

choices.why: Glossary term; Basil refers to the interpretive method he will reject when it denies the literal sense.
Renders the compound noun literally, emphasizing the act of making the world, consistent with the glossary's 'made' for ποιέω.
Preserves the reverent term λόγια for Scripture as divine utterances, matching Basil's contrast with human wisdom.

choices.english: the wisdom that has been made foolish
choices.why: Echoes 1 Corinthians 1:20 language; the passive participle is rendered literally to keep the divine action implied.
The aorist passive participle of παρατρέπω means turning aside or distorting; 'twisting' captures the polemical force against allegorizers.
The verbal adjective in -τέος expresses necessity; the negative is preserved exactly.

pass_b_english: So the longer I hold you here, the longer I withdraw you from evils. What I have said is enough for a fair-minded judge—unless he looks not at the wealth of creation but at the weakness of my own ability, and at what is sufficient for the joy of those who have gathered. The earth welcomed you with its own plants; the sea with its fish; the air with its birds. The dry land is ready to display in return things equal in honor to these. But let this be the measure of the morning feast, so that excessive fullness does not make you dull for the enjoyment of the evening. May he who filled all things with his creation, and who left in all things clear reminders of his own wonders for us, fill your hearts with all spiritual joy, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, forever and ever. Amen.

How did the morning table of words appear to you? For my part, it occurred to me to compare my own efforts to the hospitality of some poor host who, eager to be thought a fine entertainer, wearies his guests by the lack of costlier dishes, piling his meager provisions lavishly on the table—so that his ambition turns into a reproach for tastelessness. Something like that is true of us too, unless you say otherwise. But whatever it may be, you must not despise it. For the people of that time did not reject Elisha as a poor host, even though he entertained his friends with wild vegetables.

I know the rules of allegory—not because I discovered them myself, but because I have encountered the labors of others. Those who do not accept the ordinary meanings of what is written say that water is not water but some other nature, and they interpret plant and fish according to their own fancy, and they explain the origin of reptiles and wild beasts by twisting them into their own private notions—just as dream interpreters make their explanations of what appears in sleep-visions fit their own purpose. But when I hear grass, I understand grass, and plant, and fish, and wild beast, and cattle—I take everything just as it is said. For I am not ashamed of the gospel (Romans 1:16).

Nor is it because those who have written about the world have said many things about the shapes of the earth—whether the earth is a sphere, or a cylinder, or like a disk, and whether it is turned equally on all sides, or is winnowing-fan-shaped and hollow in the middle (for the writers about the world have been carried into all these notions, each one demolishing the others)—I will not for that reason be led to call our world-making less honorable, just because Moses, the servant of God, said nothing about shapes, nor said that the earth's circumference is one hundred eighty thousand stadia, nor measured how far its shadow extends through the air when the sun moves beneath the earth, nor how this shadow, when it reaches the moon, produces eclipses. Since he passed over in silence the things that are of no use to us, shall I for this reason consider the oracles of the Spirit less honorable than the wisdom that has been made foolish (1 Corinthians 1:20)? Or rather, shall I glorify him who did not occupy our minds with vain things, but arranged for everything to be written for the building up and perfecting of our souls? Some people, it seems to me, have not understood this, and with certain derivations and figurative interpretations they have attempted to attach a certain dignity from their own thinking to what is written.
notes: The source text has 'ἀντε πιδείξασθαι' which appears to be a typographical or OCR error for 'ἀντεπιδείξασθαι' (to display in return).
The source text has 'γεγραμ μένων' with a space, likely OCR damage for 'γεγραμμένων' (things written).

problems.quote: The dry land is ready to display things equal in honor to these
problems.source_quote: Ἑτοίμη ἡ χέρσος, ὁμότιμα τούτοις ἀντεπιδείξασθαι
problems.why: ἀντεπιδείξασθαι means 'to display in return/rivalry,' not merely 'display'; competitive reciprocity lost.
problems.fix: The dry land is ready to display in return things equal in honor to these

problems.quote: with their digressions and figurative turns
problems.why: παραγωγαῖς means 'derivations' (grammatical/etymological derivations), not 'digressions'; τροπολογίαις means 'tropes/figurative expressions,' but the pair refers to allegorical techniques.
problems.fix: with certain derivations and figurative expressions
problems.ruling: παραγωγαῖς = 'derivations/paragoges' (allegorical technique), not 'digressions' (παρεκβάσεις). Misleads reader about method described.

edits.old: The dry land is ready to display things equal in honor to these
edits.new: The dry land is ready to display in return things equal in honor to these

edits.old: with their digressions and figurative turns
edits.new: with certain derivations and figurative expressions

fixed: ἀντεπιδείξασθαι includes the reciprocal prefix ἀντι-, so 'display in return' is correct.
παραγωγαῖς means 'derivations' (etymological or grammatical), not 'digressions'; τροπολογίαις is 'figurative expressions' or 'tropes'.

problems.quote: the longer I keep you away from harm
problems.source_quote: ἐπὶ πλέον ἐστὶν ὑμᾶς τῶν κακῶν ὑπεξάγειν
problems.why: ὑπεξάγειν means 'withdraw/lead away from,' not 'keep away from harm'; κακῶν is genitive of separation, not 'harm' but 'evils' meaning the evils of the world or the day's troubles
problems.fix: the longer I withdraw you from worldly troubles

problems.quote: wears out his guests because he cannot afford more expensive fare
problems.source_quote: ἀπορίᾳ τῶν πολυτελεστέρων ἀποκναίει τοὺς δαιτυμόνας
problems.why: ἀποκναίει means 'wearies/exhaustes' by excessive quantity, not 'wears out'; the problem is overabundance of cheap food, not unaffordability of expensive food
problems.fix: wearies his guests by the lack of costlier dishes, piling his meager provisions lavishly
problems.ruling: ἀπορίᾳ τῶν πολυτελεστέρων = 'lacking costlier fare'; 'cannot afford' overstates; ἀποκναίει = 'wearies,' not 'wears out'.

problems.quote: with certain derivations and figurative expressions
problems.why: παραγωγαῖς means 'derivations/etymological derivations,' but τροπολογίαις means 'figurative interpretations/tropological readings,' not 'figurative expressions'—these are methods of interpretation, not expressions
problems.fix: with certain derivations and figurative interpretations
problems.ruling: τροπολογίαις = 'tropological/moral interpretations,' methods of reading; 'figurative expressions' misleads—these are interpretive methods, not expressions.

last_rejected.quote: and at what is sufficient for the joy of those who have gathered.
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ πρὸς τὸ αὔταρκες εἰς εὐφροσύνην τῶν συνεληλυθότων.
last_rejected.why: The English drops the contrast: judge by weakness of ability AND sufficiency for joy, not by wealth of creation.
last_rejected.fix: and at what suffices for the joy of those who have gathered.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'unless he looks not at...but at...and at' preserves contrast; 'what is sufficient' renders τὸ αὔταρκες adequately.

last_rejected.quote: The dry land is ready to display in return things equal in honor to these
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἑτοίμη ἡ χέρσος, ὁμότιμα τούτοις ἀντεπιδείξασθαι

last_rejected.fix: The dry land is ready to rival them with displays of equal honor
last_rejected.ruling: ἑτοίμη with ἀντεπιδείξασθαι: 'ready to display in return' captures active rivalry adequately; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: wearies his guests by the lack of costlier dishes
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀπορίᾳ τῶν πολυτελεστέρων ἀποκναίει τοὺς δαιτυμόνας
last_rejected.why: ἀποκναίει means 'wears out/exhausts,' not 'wearies' in sense of boredom; ἀπορίᾳ is 'want/scarcity,' not 'lack' as mere absence
last_rejected.fix: wears out his guests through scarcity of costlier dishes
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποκναίει 'wearies' and ἀπορίᾳ 'lack' are within normal range; 'scarcity' vs 'lack' is preference.

last_rejected.quote: piling his meager provisions lavishly on the table
last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν πενιχρὰν παρασκευὴν δαψιλῶς ἐπιφέρων τῇ τραπέζῃ
last_rejected.why: ἐπιφέρων means 'bringing upon/inflicting,' suggesting forced abundance, not neutral 'piling'; δαψιλῶς is ironically excessive
last_rejected.fix: lavishly inflicting his meager fare upon the table
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιφέρων 'bringing upon' and δαψιλῶς 'lavishly' capture the ironic excess; 'piling' is adequate rendering.

last_rejected.quote: For the people of that time did not reject Elisha as a poor host
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐδὲ γὰρ Ἐλισσαῖον ὡς φαῦλον ἑστιάτορα παρῃτοῦντο οἱ τότε
last_rejected.why: παρῃτοῦντο means 'refused/declined,' not 'reject' as ongoing attitude; ὡς φαῦλον is 'as a bad' host, 'poor' weakens the moral judgment
last_rejected.fix: For those at that time did not refuse Elisha as a bad host
last_rejected.ruling: παρῃτοῦντο 'reject' and φαῦλον 'poor/bad' are within normal range; no meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: I know the rules of allegory
last_rejected.why: νόμους here means 'methods/principles' or even 'tricks,' not 'rules'; 'rules' suggests legitimate system
last_rejected.fix: I know the tricks of allegory
last_rejected.ruling: νόμους 'rules' is standard for 'methods/principles'; no misleading change in meaning.

last_rejected.quote: the origin of reptiles and wild beasts
last_rejected.why: γένεσιν here refers to 'kinds/genera' being interpreted, not 'origin'; they twist the categories themselves
last_rejected.fix: the kinds of reptiles and wild beasts
last_rejected.ruling: γένεσιν can mean 'origin/creation'; context is interpreting Genesis creation, so 'origin' is defensible.

last_rejected.quote: whether it is turned equally on all sides
last_rejected.why: ἀποτετόρνευται means 'turned on a lathe,' i.e., perfectly spherical; 'turned equally' obscures the technical term
last_rejected.fix: whether it is lathe-turned equally on all sides
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποτετόρνευται 'turned' with ἐξίσου 'equally' conveys lathe-turned spherical sense; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: winnowing-fan-shaped and hollow in the middle
last_rejected.why: λικνοειδής means 'shaped like a winnowing-fan' (concave), but μεσόκοιλος specifies 'hollow in the middle' as result; English suggests two separate things
last_rejected.ruling: λικνοειδής 'winnowing-fan-shaped' and μεσόκοιλος 'hollow in middle' both rendered; 'and' linking is acceptable.

last_rejected.quote: the wisdom that has been made foolish
last_rejected.why: μωρανθείσης is passive 'made foolish,' but context is 1 Cor 1:20 where God makes worldly wisdom foolish; 'that has been made foolish' is ambiguous
last_rejected.fix: the wisdom that God has made foolish
last_rejected.ruling: μωρανθείσης 'made foolish' is correct passive; 1 Cor 1:20 reference is noted; no real error.

last_rejected.quote: with certain derivations and figurative interpretations
last_rejected.why: παραγωγαῖς means 'derivations' in grammatical sense (etymological tricks), 'trope-interpretations' is technical; 'figurative interpretations' loses specificity
last_rejected.fix: with certain derivations and tropological readings
last_rejected.ruling: παραγωγαῖς 'derivations' and τροπολογίαις 'figurative interpretations' are reasonable renderings; specificity not lost.

last_rejected.quote: attach a certain dignity from their own thinking to what is written
last_rejected.source_quote: σεμνότητά τινα ἐκ τῆς οἰκείας αὐτῶν διανοίας ἐπεχείρησαν τοῖς γεγραμμένοις ἐπιφημίσαι
last_rejected.why: ἐπιφημίσαι means 'to affix a label/name,' i.e., impose a reputation; 'attach dignity' suggests adding real value, not imposing false reputation
last_rejected.fix: attempted to affix a certain prestige from their own minds to what is written
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιφημίσαι 'attach/impose' with σεμνότητα 'dignity' captures meaning; 'attach' implies imposition adequately.
